## [2.15.4] - 2026-11-06

### Changed
- **Hermes runtime moves to v0.23.0 on Python 3.14.** The carried Hermes patch set is re-based onto v0.23.0: `0007` (holographic memory removal) and `0008` (board argument over env override) are dropped because upstream absorbed both, `0011` (fresh `started_at` on claim, cleared on reclaim) and `0012` (out-of-tree worktree root) are regenerated, and all seven remaining patches apply on their own to pristine v0.23.0. The compatibility audit behind it is `docs/audits/2026-11-06-hermes-0.23-compat.md` (patch verdicts, integration points, behaviour changes, cutover recipe).

### Fixed
- **Proxy relaunch can no longer pick Python 3.14 for LiteLLM.** The daemon
  launches `sparkrun proxy start` / orphan repair with `UV_PYTHON=3.12` unless
  the operator already exported `UV_PYTHON`, so uv's machine-global default can
  no longer break uvloop on :4000. `hscc doctor` warns when `uv python find
  --no-project` resolves >= 3.14 with no `UV_PYTHON` pin.
- **v0.23.0 runtime rebuild docs corrected.** The compatibility audit's cutover
  checklist now uses the uv-managed 3.14 sync recipe, the optional-package
  freeze diff (`xpress9` excluded), the `hscc-cli` install, and records the
  32 -> 52 config migrations that reset personality/delegation/curator values.
- **README lint index + repo-wide import-order guard.** Indexed the Hermes
  v0.23.0 compatibility audit in `docs/README.md`, and the standalone-import
  guard now skips `.worktrees/` just like pytest's `norecursedirs`.
- **Queued REPL messages use `/queue add`, so text can never manage the queue.**
  `hscc-api/repl_inject.py` sent `"/queue " + text`; Hermes v0.22+ parses
  `/queue list|clear|edit N|rm N|move A B` as queue management, so a queued
  message starting with one of those words could wipe or edit the orchestrator's
  queue. The explicit `add` form always enqueues (upstream
  `hermes_cli/cli_loops_mixin.py`), and a regression test pins `"clear the
  board"` arriving as `/queue add clear the board`.
- **`hscc verify` accepts `multiplex_profiles` under `gateway:` as well as at
  the top level.** Hermes v0.23.0 may migrate the flag to
  `gateway.multiplex_profiles` and pop the top-level key, which made
  `check_config_wiring` report a false `missing: multiplex_profiles`. Both
  shapes now pass; missing in both still fails.
- **`hscc api install-service` writes a version-stable WorkingDirectory.**
  The launchd unit pinned the brew Cellar keg path
  (`<prefix>/Cellar/hscc/<ver>/libexec/hscc/hscc-api`), which `brew upgrade`
  deletes, leaving launchd unable to start the API (exit 78 EX_CONFIG). A
  keg-shaped path is now rewritten to `<prefix>/opt/hscc/<same suffix>`;
  non-brew layouts are unchanged.
## [2.15.3] - 2026-11-05

### Added
- **A new daemon stream catches alive-but-starved model streams (incident 2026-11-05).**
  `stream_silence.check_stream_silence` runs every 60 s and compares each
  running kanban card's own worker session against the newest `latency=`
  completion line in that profile's `agent.log`. Cards are matched to their
  session by the line's `[session_id]` and the session's spawn timestamp versus
  the run's `started_at` (the `card-stats.py` rule), so one card's completion
  cannot mask a silent sibling; an ambiguous match is reported `○` (unknown),
  never fresh. Orchestrators are judged alive and busy-in-a-turn from their
  tmux pane through `repl_inject` (`msg=interrupt` = busy, bare prompt = idle,
  no pane = dead-pane suppression) — log mtime is not a heartbeat, so
  housekeeping lines cannot page and an idle orchestrator at its prompt is
  never starved however old its last call. A busy orchestrator or running card
  whose last completion is older than the 600 s threshold gets a WARN log
  line, a persisted state entry, and one desktop notify per 30-minute
  per-session cooldown. The stream always publishes `ok: true`; `hscc verify`
  gains a `stream_silence` row that lists the ages and is never red by itself.
  Tests are hermetic (fabricated tmp logs and fake roster/notify/state seams).

### Fixed
- **`routes_profile.hermes_root_dir` now uses the shared `is_profile_dir`
  predicate.** The profile-dir filter in the `hermes_homes()` ladder had been
  spelled inline, so it could drift from the canonical profiles-grandparent
  rule in `hscc_daemon/hermes_python.py`. Behaviour is unchanged; the filter is
  now pinned structurally and by a hermetic skip test.
- **`enable_plugins.py` / `install_soul.py` seeded the caller's PROFILE when
  bootstrap ran from a profile session.** Both `__main__` entries joined
  `HERMES_HOME` directly, but Hermes exports it as `<root>/profiles/<name>` in
  its normal profile mode, so bootstrap wrote `<profile>/config.yaml` /
  `<profile>/SOUL.md` and the ROOT install stayed unseeded (audit t_8893ab89
  finding 3). Both entries now resolve the Hermes ROOT with the shared
  profiles-grandparent rule (`backup_util._hermes_root`, the same rung as
  `hscc_daemon.hermes_python.hermes_homes` and the F2 landing in
  `install_review_skill`), and gained a documented `--home` flag that is used
  exactly as given for an intentional profile wire. The import-time and
  plugin-runtime joins the audit classified PROFILE-intent are untouched.
- **`hscc api install-service` refused to run from every Hermes profile session.**
  Hermes exports `HERMES_HOME=<root>/profiles/<name>` whenever it runs under a
  profile — its normal run mode — and `hermes-agent` (where the venv lives) sits at
  the ROOT. `api_launchd.recommend_api_python()` joined the two
  (`HERMES_HOME + "hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3"`), so from any profile session it
  resolved a path that cannot exist, returned `None`, and the verb died with
  `error: no Hermes venv python found (HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3)`.
  The 2026-11-04 API migration had to work around it with `env -u HERMES_HOME`, which
  is a hint about the resolver, not the install. Resolution now goes through the new
  shared `hscc_daemon/hermes_python.py`: exported `$HERMES_HOME` (a profile-local
  checkout still wins), then the `profiles/`-grandparent root, then `~/.hermes`, then
  the venv the running process is inside — the same `profiles/` rule
  `hscc-bootstrap/doctor.py:hermes_root_from_home` and `hscc-roles/rolelib.py` already
  use. Still fail-closed: `None` when NO candidate exists, and the refusal now names
  every path it searched instead of the one path that could never be there. The
  install stays opt-in (write the plist, never `launchctl bootstrap`).
  **Audit of the sibling the docstring cited (`bootstrap._api_python`): that function
  does not exist anywhere in the repo** (`git grep _api_python` finds only
  `recommend_api_python` and prose references), so the docstring pointed at a stale
  name. The sibling that really did share the flaw is the shell one:
  `hscc-bootstrap/bootstrap.sh` resolved `PYBIN="$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python"`
  the same way, silently fell through to a brew `python3` from a profile session, and
  then handed that brew python to `install_cli.py "$PYBIN"` — installing the `hscc`
  console shim into brew python instead of the Hermes venv. It walks the same ladder
  now, with a shell-level test that sources the extracted block. `$PLUGINS`
  deliberately keeps the raw profile-scoped home: Hermes scans
  `get_hermes_home()/plugins`, so widening it would make the payload undiscoverable.
- **`enable_plugins` wrote node-direct auxiliary URLs into orch profiles; now derived from serving.json + repaired + pinned.** The orchestrator profile's 9 auxiliary endpoints (compression + the 8 text tasks: kanban_decomposer, triage_specifier, profile_describer, curator, title_generation, skills_hub, approval, mcp) carried `base_url: http://<orch node>:8000/v1` while model/delegation/goal_judge correctly carried the local proxy — so every auxiliary call for the orchestrator profile (compression included) died on an address the gateway cannot route to. Culprit: `COMPACT_URL`'s default `http://{ORCH_MODEL_HOST}:8000/v1` (a hardcoded constant), stamped by `_ensure_compaction` (1 entry) and `_ensure_text_auxiliaries` (8). `cluster_template.py` (its :2316/:2776 never touch an auxiliary block; routing resolves proxied families to `localhost:<proxy>`) and `hscc-roles/generator.py` (orch profiles get no `auxiliary` block at all) are ruled out with tests. Three fixes: (1) `_serving_compact_route()` derives the endpoint from `serving.json` — proxy + worker alias under `uniform_pool`, the direct orchestrator endpoint on a pinned fleet, the old constant only as the no-serving.json bootstrap fallback; (2) a narrow repair for the poison this generator itself left on disk (a base_url whose host is a fleet node on a pool fleet — unreachable by construction) that fill-empty could never fix, because every later bootstrap and every `doctor --fix` read the wrong value as a deliberate operator choice — deliberate cloud/localhost/pinned providers are still preserved byte-for-byte and the repair is idempotent; (3) the `check_profile_endpoints` pin hole closed: under a pool the node origin from serving.json is no longer an allowed hermes route and the finding names the profile, the dotted key path, and the fleet shape. 27 new tests (15 bootstrap derivation/repair/preservation, 5 generator-plan, 7 guard-teeth), all tmp-dir with synthetic addresses.
- **The profiles-grandparent Hermes ROOT rule now has one definition.**
  `hscc_daemon/hermes_python.hermes_root` (plus the named `is_profile_dir`
  predicate) is canonical; `backup_util._hermes_root`,
  `rolelib._hermes_root` and `doctor.hermes_root_from_home` delegate to it
  through the guarded deferred import, keeping a same-rule fallback where
  `hscc_daemon` is not importable. The transform stays deterministic (no
  first-existing probing) and every caller's profile-home and plain-root
  behavior is unchanged.
- **`hscc-model-onboard` mirrored `model.default` against `<profile>/profiles` —
  silently skipping every profile under a profile session.** `onboard.py` bound
  `HERMES_HOME`/`HERMES_CONFIG`/`PROFILES_DIR` at import from `$HERMES_HOME`.
  Hermes exports that as the *profile* dir (`<root>/profiles/<name>`) for every
  profile session, so `PROFILES_DIR` resolved to `<profile>/profiles` — a path
  that does not exist — and the per-profile mirroring walked nothing while
  editing the profile's own `config.yaml` as if it were the root: the real root
  config and all sibling profiles kept the old model, with a green
  "model.default updated" line printed (audit t_8893ab89 finding 5). The root is
  now resolved at **call time** through the shared homes ladder
  (`hscc_daemon.hermes_python.hermes_homes`, t_314eb13c; guarded standalone
  fallback + drift pin, same pattern as `apply_patches.py` /
  `ensure_review_feature.py`), excluding any `profiles/<name>` candidate (a
  profile dir has its own `config.yaml`, so a marker test alone cannot tell it
  from a root). `$HSCC_HERMES_ROOT` is the explicit operator override.
  An unresolvable home is now **reported** (with the paths ruled out) instead of
  reading as a no-op, `backup_configs` snapshots the root config and EVERY
  profile config (the old set hard-coded one `worker` profile from a directory
  that did not exist under a profile session), and profiles without a
  `config.yaml` are announced rather than dropped.
- **The hermes patch step silently no-oped from every profile session (the
  un-fixed siblings of c5ba9926).** `bootstrap.sh` opened its
  `Install: hermes/sparkrun patches` stage with `HERMES_DIR="$HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent"`
  (raw env join, L509) and gated the apply on
  `apply_patches.py --check` — whose own default target was
  `Path($HERMES_HOME) / "hermes-agent"` (L101-102). Hermes exports
  `HERMES_HOME=<root>/profiles/<name>` for every profile session (the fleet's
  normal run mode) and `hermes-agent` sits at the ROOT, so both joins named a
  directory that cannot exist. `--check` reported
  `{"hermes": {"ok": false, "error": ".../profiles/<name>/hermes-agent not found"}}`,
  the stage's `grep '"ok": true'` failed, and bootstrap printed
  `patches not cleanly applicable (already patched, or upstream drifted…)` —
  blaming upstream for a path that was never even checked — then skipped the
  `--target` apply. The hermes patch set (kanban review tool + resume hook)
  silently never landed. Reproduced read-only on the live box at base
  `df8253ac`: old `--check` under
  `HERMES_HOME=~/.hermes/profiles/backend-engineer` -> `ok:false`,
  `error: …/profiles/backend-engineer/hermes-agent not found`, gate `False`;
  the fixed `--check` in the same env resolves
  `target=/Users/<op>/.hermes/hermes-agent` and reports real per-patch
  verdicts. `apply_patches.py` now resolves the checkout through the shared
  homes ladder — `_load_hermes_python()` / `agent_dir_candidates()` /
  `resolve_agent_dir()`, reusing `hermes_python.hermes_agent_dir()` shipped by
  F1 (t_919ac971), with the same guarded-fallback + drift-pin pattern as
  `ensure_review_feature.py` — and echoes the chosen `target` in the JSON so
  the resolution is auditable. `bootstrap.sh` gained a `resolve_hermes_dir()`
  ladder: first the already-laddered `$PYBIN`'s venv great-grandparent
  (`$PYBIN = <checkout>/venv/bin/python*`, shape-checked against
  `hermes-agent`), falling back to the same home sites the PYBIN ladder walks
  (exported home → its `profiles/` grandparent → `~/.hermes`, each requiring a
  real DIRECTORY); the chosen candidate is reported (`ladder: pyvenv|home|profiles-root`)
  and a genuine no-checkout outcome gets its own warning —
  "the hermes/sparkrun patch sets were NOT applied" — instead of the drift
  message. The stage's `--check` now targets the SAME resolved `$HERMES_DIR`
  the apply writes to, so gate and target can no longer disagree. No raw
  `HERMES_HOME` join remains in either file's code paths (pinned by tests).
- **`ensure_review_feature.py` silently skipped the review-feature re-apply from
  every profile session.** It bound `HERMES_DIR = $HERMES_HOME/hermes-agent` at
  IMPORT (L24-25). Hermes exports `HERMES_HOME=<root>/profiles/<name>` whenever it
  runs under a profile — the fleet's normal run mode — and `hermes-agent` (the
  runtime checkout the feature is cherry-picked into) sits at the ROOT. So the
  import-time join resolved `<profile>/hermes-agent`, a path that cannot exist;
  `os.path.isdir` was false and the step returned
  `{"status": "skipped_missing", "ok": True}` (L86-87), which `bootstrap.sh` prints
  in its green case (`already_present|applied|skipped_missing`). A `hermes update`
  that dropped the PR #43425 review feature left it dropped while bootstrap
  reported a near-green row — the apply path was never even reached. Reproduced on
  the live box at base `a99a2a1a`: `HERMES_DIR=…/profiles/backend-engineer/hermes-agent`,
  `isdir` false, `ensure_review_feature()` -> `skipped_missing`/ok, while the real
  checkout at the root existed and reported the marker `absent`. The step now
  resolves the checkout **at call time** through the shared ladder — new
  `hermes_python.hermes_agent_dir()` / `agent_dir_candidates()` /
  `describe_agent_search()`, siblings of `hermes_venv_python()` reusing
  `hermes_homes()`: exported `$HERMES_HOME` (a profile-local checkout still wins),
  the `profiles/` grandparent root, then `~/.hermes`. `skipped_missing`/ok is kept
  only for the genuinely-no-install case and now carries a `detail` naming every
  candidate it ruled out, so a resolver regression can no longer read as "there is
  no runtime here". No raw env join remains and no import-time `HERMES_DIR` exists
  (pinned by a test). Deliberate difference from the interpreter ladder: the
  checkout ladder has NO running-`sys.executable` fallback — a caller *writes* into
  the resolved checkout, so the target must come from the configured home, not from
  whichever python invoked it. A guarded deferred import of `hscc_daemon` keeps a
  standalone bootstrap install working, with `_fallback_homes()` mirroring the
  ladder and a drift test pinning the two together. The marker-read
  `unreadable` path, the dirty/mid-operation refusals and the ref-token guard are
  unchanged.
- **`install_review_skill.py --skill all` missed the root home and sibling
  profiles under a profile session.** Hermes exports
  `HERMES_HOME=<root>/profiles/<name>` whenever it runs under a profile, and
  `default_home()` returned that profile path verbatim; `skill_dirs()` then
  walked `<profile>/profiles`, which does not exist, so only the current
  profile was seeded. `default_home()` now resolves the Hermes ROOT via the
  existing profiles-grandparent rule in `backup_util._hermes_root` (the same
  rule `doctor.py` and `rolelib.py` use), restoring the root skills dir plus
  every root profile. An explicit `--home` is still used exactly as given, so
  a deliberately profile-scoped install remains scoped.
- **`GET /v1/profile/list` and the profile editor enumerated ZERO profiles the moment the API inherited a profile env.** Both routes built their profiles path as `Path($HERMES_HOME or ~/.hermes)/"profiles"`. Hermes exports `HERMES_HOME=<root>/profiles/<name>` for every profile session — the fleet's normal run mode — and `profiles/` is a child of the ROOT, so the join resolved `<root>/profiles/<name>/profiles`: on this box that directory *exists and is empty* (an earlier t_7a16aed0-class leak left it behind), so the Library listed nothing and the editor 404'd every real profile — and a `PUT` would have written a fresh `config.yaml` into the double-nest, inventing a phantom profile. They were correct only by accident: the `com.hscc.api` launchd unit exports HOME + PATH and nothing else, verified against the live plist. Both now resolve the ROOT through the shared ladder `hscc_daemon.hermes_python.hermes_homes()` (`routes_profile.hermes_root_dir`, which `routes_profile_editor` delegates to — one resolver, no private copy), skipping any candidate that is itself a profile dir so the double-nest is ruled out even when it exists, and falling back to `~/.hermes` rather than to `$HERMES_HOME`. Same call-time resolution as before, so a long-lived API still reacts to env changes. The editor's "GLOBAL" skills dir — audit row 34, the same env join in the same file — went to the ROOT too, which restores the root half of the preload picker. Reproduced on the base at `df8253ac` (old resolver listed `['ghost']`, the phantom, and not the real `hscc-orch`); 9 of the 11 new tests fail there and pass here. `test_api_launchd.py` now pins the plist's env shape as exactly `{HOME, PATH}` so the accidental guard cannot quietly become load-bearing again.
- **`hscc verify`'s `api_routes` row called a healthy API dead.** In the
  installed keg the row read `route(s) the app calls did not answer: Traceback
  (most recent call last):` while the API was listening and its log was clean.
  Two faults stacked: the sweep is run by script path, so its own directory was
  the only thing on `sys.path` and `from hscc_daemon import cli_theme` raised
  `ModuleNotFoundError`; and `check_api_routes` shelled out to a bare
  `python3`, which on the keg has no `rich` at all. The traceback exited 1 and
  exit 1 meant "a route did not answer" — the checker's own crash was
  indistinguishable from the outage the row exists to catch. The sweep now
  bootstraps `sys.path` itself (the sanctioned `verify_chat_roundtrip.py`
  pattern), `verify` uses its own interpreter, and a sweep that produced no
  route report is UNVERIFIED — never a dead-route verdict. A missing client
  source, missing `curl` or unavailable renderer exits a new code 3 ("could not
  run"). The row also stops printing a traceback's useless first line: the
  exception itself is on the last.
- **`hscc verify --chat`'s deep check was dead on arrival.**
  `hscc_daemon/verify_chat_roundtrip.py` carried a `sys.path` bootstrap that was
  dead code: line 49 imported `hscc_daemon` and line 52 inserted the package
  root, so the insert ran *after* the import it was written to protect. Run the
  way `verify.run_chat_roundtrip` and the installed keg run it — a bare script
  path, so only `hscc_daemon/` lands on `sys.path` and the parent that *contains*
  the package is missing — it died before reading a single config value:
  `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'hscc_daemon'` at line 49, exit 1
  (reproduced 2026-11-04 with the repo venv interpreter, which has `rich`, so
  `rich` was never the blocker here). The bootstrap now computes the root from
  `__file__` and runs *before* the import — the shape proven for
  `api_route_sweep.py` in #213 (t_ef36fe71). `verify` tolerated the crash (`rc=1`
  fell back to the traceback text as the row detail, so the row was verbose
  rather than wrongly green), but the check it reports on never actually ran.
- **A missing renderer can no longer take the human view down.** The
  `cli_theme` import in `verify_chat_roundtrip.py` is now guarded, and
  `render_human` falls back to `_render_plain` — the same fixed labels, no Rich.
  With no `rich` in the interpreter running us, the round trip still runs,
  `--json` stays byte-identical (verify's path is renderer-proof) and the human
  view prints plain text instead of raising `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object
  has no attribute 'make_console'` out of `render_human`. The exit code stays the
  round trip's own verdict, so a missing colour scheme is never reported as a
  chat failure.

  suppression, empty roster, unknown signal, bounded log-tail parsing of
  `latency=` vs `Stream stale`, never-red verify row, a busy orchestrator with

  fresh housekeeping lines, two sessions in one log warn only for the silent

  `_fallback_homes` == `hermes_python.hermes_homes` + `hermes-agent` over four env
  shapes; module has no import-time `HERMES_DIR`.
- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_hermes_python.py`: 19 -> **25** cases for the checkout
  ladder (profile home finds the root checkout, profile-local checkout wins,
  fail-closed `None`, a stale `hermes-agent` *file* is not a checkout, no
  running-interpreter path is invented, `describe_agent_search` names every
  candidate).
- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_api_route_sweep_standalone.py`: **15** new cases —
  the operator's manual repro (bare script path, cwd `/`, scrubbed `HOME`, fake
  keg in tmp) plus every classification path through `check_api_routes`, and
  both false-verdict traps (a crash read as red, an empty route list read as
  green). Mutation-checked: removing the `sys.path` bootstrap turns
  `test_bare_script_run_can_import_the_real_theme` red.
- Live-keg reproduction of both faults before the fix, and of the fixed sweep
  after: `--json` on a closed loopback port reports its routes, the human view
  without `rich` says `cannot render`, an absent `curl` or an empty route list
  says `could not run`, and none of them emits a traceback.
- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_chat_roundtrip_standalone.py` (11 cases) runs the
  script by bare script path from a cwd outside the repo with a scrubbed `HOME`,
  no `hscc` on `PATH` and `PYTHONPATH` dropped so the child cannot inherit the
  real repo for free, and asserts it never dies with `ModuleNotFoundError`. It
  asserts on the preconditions path (no API host/token → exit 2 + parseable
  error), so **no real chat prompt is ever fired at the live orchestrator**; a
  fake keg in `tmp_path` supplies the package, and the real `cli_theme.py`
  planted in it proves the Rich panel actually draws from a bare script path
  (delete the bootstrap and that case goes red). Six mutation probes in a
  throwaway clone — bootstrap-after-import, bootstrap deleted, unguarded theme
  import, fallback renderer removed, fallback lying about the exit code, AST
  guard neutered — all KILLED, each reverted before the next.
- The repo was swept for the same ordering fault with an AST statement-order
  check (a module-level `import hscc_daemon` before the first module-level
  `sys.path` call, function-level lazy imports excluded), and the check now
  *ships as a test* so the report cannot rot: any bare-runnable module that
  reintroduces bootstrap-after-import fails the suite with `file:line`. The
  checker was first validated against the known-bad file so a false "all clean"
  was impossible. **Only one module had the ordering bug — this one.** Three
  others import `hscc_daemon` from a bare-runnable file with no bootstrap at all
  and are accounted for, not silently refactored: `api_route_sweep.py`
  (unguarded import and no bootstrap on `main`; its fix ships in #213 and is
  untouched here), `event_driven.py` (peer-guarded import with a
  `_FallbackTheme`, so a bare path renders unthemed instead of crashing) and
  `hscc.py` (launched with `PYTHONPATH` pointed at the package root by its
  launchd/systemd unit in `hscc_daemon/install.py` and by
  `hscc-bootstrap/restart_daemon.sh`, whose own comments record this exact
  `ModuleNotFoundError`).
## [2.15.2] - 2026-11-04

### Added
- **`install_payload` now writes the HSCC payload into a selected set of
  profile homes.** The selector used to skip every profile home that did not
  already carry a `plugins/` dir — on this fleet exactly 2 of 49 homes were
  ever written, so 47 homes (including dispatched ones: `ios-engineer`,
  `worker`, `qa`) silently never received the payload and the budget-hook
  doctor row correctly read red for them. The selection is now an explicit
  allowlist, `target_profiles` in `~/.hscc/target_profiles.json` (operator
  decision option 3 on t_16eb73ab): absent file → the seeded default (the hscc
  board's own assignees, 13 names); `["*", ...]` → every home, so option 1
  stays one config edit away; `[]` → the old skip-everything behaviour. A
  dedicated file rather than a key inside `cluster.json` because
  `hscc-cluster/discovery.py::_write_cache` rewrites `cluster.json` from a
  freshly built dict on every live discovery — an operator's widening edit
  there would silently evaporate. A selected home
  gets its `plugins/` created, and the per-home summary reports
  `created: true|false` so the bootstrap run can name exactly which homes
  flipped from payload-less to payload. A malformed value keeps the seeded
  default and surfaces `target_profiles_error` on the summary — a silently
  ignored allowlist looks exactly like a working one.
- **`hscc api install-service` now carries the bind flags into the launchd
  unit.** `hscc api install-service [--tailscale] [--bind <ip>] [--port <n>]`
  writes those flags into the unit's `ProgramArguments`, so migrating a
  tailnet-served API onto launchd no longer silently drops the bind. The flags
  are validated at install time exactly the way `api_cli` parses them for
  `start` (last-wins collapsed to one, `0.0.0.0`/`::` refused, `--port` must be
  a real port) — a bad combination is refused with `error:` before the plist
  file is touched, never baked into a unit that would fail at boot.
  `--no-qr` is deliberately NOT forwarded: it is display-only and a launchd
  unit has no terminal. No flags keeps the unit byte-identical to before.
- **`launchd-setup.sh render-only [OUT]`** — renders the plist from the
  template and exits before any launchctl interaction. The plist render moved
  out of a bare `sed` into a `render_plist` function with a
  `__TMUX_ENV__` template placeholder, giving the install path a test seam
  that never installs or loads a job. `hscc_daemon/tests/
  test_launchd_setup_tmux_env.py` drives the real script through the seam and
  parses the result with `plistlib` (the first test harness this script ever
  had — the card believed one existed; `grep -rn launchd-setup
  hscc_daemon/tests/` was empty).

### Changed
- **A new doctor row is now one edit in one place, not three hunks in the same
  file.** `hscc-bootstrap/doctor.py::run_doctor()` had become a merge hotspot:
  every feature that wanted a row edited the *same* three places — a row adapter
  appended after the previous one, a seam keyword appended to the signature, and
  an entry (plus its "why this row exists" comment) appended to the `checks`
  list. PR #175 vs #173 collided in all three and needed the t_3f805c4f rebase,
  and PR #175 collided with this refactor's own branch the same way while it was
  being written. The wiring is now `FEATURE_CHECK_ROWS` — one
  `doctor_rows.FeatureCheckRow` entry per row (its key, its seam keyword, and the
  hooks that produce its verdict), iterated by `run_doctor()`. New rows arrive
  their seam through `**feature_rows` and are validated against the registry, so
  a typo'd seam is a `TypeError` rather than a silently ignored keyword that
  downgrades a row to its refusal verdict, and the signature never grows again.
  Row hooks are resolved against the doctor module **per call**, so the suites
  that patch `_load_orch_waker` / `_kanban_enforce_check_row` on the module keep
  pinning what they pin. Each row declares the per-row context it reads —
  `hscc_dir` (the sandboxed `~/.hscc` root) or `hermes_home` (the deployed plugin
  tree the budget row reads) — so a row can never be handed a keyword its
  function does not accept. No check semantics moved: same three-source trust
  order (injected seam → in-suite refusal → the feature's own `doctor_check`),
  same pytest fence, same *unverifiable* row for a module that cannot be
  imported, same five-field `Check` adapter, same row order — the five feature
  suites (`test_doctor_orch_waker`, `_cron_watchers`, `_supervision`,
  `_kanban_enforce`, `_budget_hook`) pass unchanged. New suite
  `test_doctor_row_registry.py` (17 tests) pins what a registry loses to a direct
  call and what the move could break: every hook name an entry names exists on
  the module, the seam map agrees with the signature, a row appended to the list
  renders with **no** change to `run_doctor()` (mutation-proven: pinning the
  loop to the known rows fails it), an unknown seam keyword raises
  (mutation-proven), and the budget row receives `hermes_home` and never
  `hscc_dir` (mutation-proven: dropping the kwarg from the render call fails it).
- **The reviewer role no longer cards its own follow-ups.** `roles/reviewer.yaml`
  states the operator's standing rule as role identity, so it is part of the
  SOUL every reviewer session is generated with: a follow-up found on the way
  (an adjacent defect, a cleanup, something worth doing later) is commented on
  **the card under review** and that card is returned to `todo`, so the
  orchestrator decides whether it becomes work — spawning new cards from a
  review is named as forbidden, and says why (`kanban_create` is not a
  reviewer's tool; decomposition belongs to the orchestrator). Before this the
  rule existed only as a correction after the fact, so every reviewer session
  rediscovered the choice on its own and a review could silently mint cards the
  orchestrator never routed. Rule text lives in the spec `identity`, not in a
  hand-edited live SOUL, because `role_soul_check.py` exists precisely to warn
  that a hand-appended block is deleted by the next `hscc.py generate`.

### Fixed
- **`python -m api_server serve` was a no-op.** The launchd unit's
  `ProgramArguments` run that command, but `api_server` had no `__main__`
  block: the module imported, registered its routes and exited 0 without ever
  binding a socket, so a boot-loaded unit would have respun forever under
  `KeepAlive` while the API stayed offline. `api_server` now has a real
  `main()` entrypoint (`serve` + the same `--tailscale`/`--bind`/`--port`
  flags), serves through `create_server()` so the bind rules and fail-closed
  token load cannot drift from `hscc api start`, exits non-zero on any startup
  refusal (that is what tells launchd the unit failed), and shuts the
  gateway sidecar down on SIGTERM so a boot-time stop cannot orphan
  `hermes serve` on 9119. Deliberately writes no PID file: the documented
  "trust launchctl, not the PID file" asymmetry is kept, because an
  `api.pid` would let `hscc api stop` SIGTERM a supervised process that
  `KeepAlive` then resurrects.
- **`python -m api_server` 404d every route except `/v1/ping`.** Running a
  module with `-m` executes it as `__main__`, but every `routes_*.py` imports
  `api_server` by name — so the same file was imported a second time and the
  routes registered on that other module instance, while the listening process
  served from the `__main__` instance whose table held only the inline ping
  route. `api_server` now aliases `sys.modules["api_server"]` to itself when
  run as `__main__`. Pinned without executing a handler: a GET on the
  POST-only `/v1/profile/install` must be 405 (registered), not 404.
- **The launchd install path shipped a pane-blind daemon: the orch-waker
  could never see a tmux pane.** launchd starts the daemon with a CLEAN
  environment, and the plist template's `EnvironmentVariables` carried only
  PATH/HOME/PYTHONPATH/PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE — never `TMUX_TMPDIR`, which
  is where the operator's real tmux server (iTerm2 integration) puts its
  socket (`~/.tmux/tmp`). `repl_inject` found no server, so the waker
  delivered to ZERO panes for its whole existence (2,283 audit lines, zero
  ok=true, measured live 2026-11-03) while every board burned retries on
  `FAILED no tmux pane` — the same symptom as the dead-pane case of
  `t_f1122b7a` but caused by the *supervisor environment*, invisible to the
  dead-pane backoff's per-board logic. `launchd-setup.sh` now propagates
  `TMUX_TMPDIR` from the installing shell into the plist when it is set
  (XML-escaped; omitted entirely when unset or empty — an empty value would
  point tmux at `""`, worse than absent).
- **`hscc-cluster/plugin.yaml` now declares its 6 hooks; the drift suite
  guards hooks as it already guards tools.** The manifest carried
  `provides_tools` (the GAP-A-7 registry-first list) and no hook block at
  all, so `hermes plugins doctor` WARNed every registered hook —
  `kanban_task_claimed`/`_blocked`/`_completed`, `pre_tool_call` (workflow.py),
  `post_api_request`/`transform_tool_result` (budget_watch.py) — as "not
  listed in provides_hooks" (6 WARNs; found by qa during t_1153d42c live
  acceptance). Registration always succeeded (doctor OK: 23 tools, 6 hooks),
  so this is declaration hygiene: Hermes advertises and audits capabilities
  from the manifest, and a manifest that omits what it registers lies in the
  same direction GAP-A-7 was about. `provides_hooks` now mirrors the
  `ctx.register_hook(...)` calls exactly, annotated per source module. The
  repo has no other plugin that registers a hook, so no other manifest needed
  the block.
- **`hscc cluster` silently deleted the operator's `node_recovery` opt-outs.**
  `discovery._write_cache` wrote `to_cluster_json(topo)` — `name`/`gateway`/
  `workers`/`nasDevices` and nothing else — over `~/.hscc/cluster.json` on
  every successful live discovery, so every hand-added top-level key
  evaporated on the next sweep. That is exactly where
  `install_autoreboot` / `install_notifier_mask` / `install_gpu_clock_cap` /
  `node_recovery` read their opt-outs and where `bootstrap.sh` tells operators
  to write them: one discovery run deleted an opt-out and the layer silently
  re-enabled, which looks identical to a working opt-out. `_write_cache` now
  re-reads the file it is about to replace and carries forward every top-level
  key it does not own (`OWNED_CACHE_KEYS`), so `node_recovery` — and any key a
  future card adds — survives. Ownership rather than an allowlist of keys to
  keep, and owned keys always come from the live topology, so a hand-edited
  `workers` list can never resurrect a node removed from the sparkrun cluster.
  A `cluster.json` that exists but cannot be read is no longer overwritten in
  silence: the rewrite still happens (the cache write stays best-effort) but
  names on stderr what is about to be lost.
- **Step 4 of the dep-bump runbook never stated the signal the guard calls
  decisive.** `FORK_RULE_LINES` tells the verifier to "confirm the balancer is
  live in `~/.cache/sparkrun/proxy/litellm_config.yaml`:
  `litellm_settings.callbacks` contains `sparkrun_balancer.handler` and
  `sparkrun_balancer.py` sits next to the config", and calls that callback the
  live signal. The operator runbook
  (`install/hscc-skills/hscc/references/runtime-bump-verification.md`) step 4
  said only that `router_settings` propagates, `proxy_router_settings` /
  `router_drift` must be quiet, and `simple-shuffle` is HEALTHY — so an
  operator following it literally never opened the callbacks line. In the one
  scenario the guard exists for (the balancer silently stops being emitted
  while `router_settings` still propagates, e.g. `sparkrun_balancer.py` is not
  next to the config) every step-4 signal stays green.
  `git log -S "sparkrun_balancer.handler" -- <runbook>` returns zero commits:
  the omission is pre-existing, not a regression t_6956da89 introduced — that
  card's pin correctly forbids CONTRADICTION while letting the runbook say
  less, and this closes the "says less" half. Step 4 (and the rule-2 failure
  description and the `simple-shuffle` NOTE sentence, which are the other two
  places a reader meets `simple-shuffle`/`litellm_config.yaml`) now state the
  callbacks check beside the `router_settings` check.
  `TestRunbookAgreesWithGuard` gained
  `test_runbook_states_the_balancer_live_signal_the_guard_calls_decisive`: it
  selects the canonical line by SHAPE (the only `FORK_RULE_LINES` entry naming
  both a generated `.yaml` and a `.py` — `_balancer_line`), derives the
  required identifiers from that line's code tokens (dotted callback paths plus
  the module file; `_balancer_signal_ids`), derives the base-strategy value from
  its `key: value` token (`_base_strategy_value`) and the config name from its
  `.yaml` token, then requires every runbook sentence naming the generated
  config or that strategy to carry all of them — per-sentence, so naming the
  callback once in an unrelated paragraph cannot satisfy it. No obligation is
  restated as a literal here. Proven to bite with 13 mutants in a throwaway
  worktree — 11 RED, each on the leg meant to catch it, 2 GREEN negative
  controls, every mutant restored with `__pycache__` wiped so CPython's
  (mtime,size) check could not serve stale bytecode: drop the new step-4
  sentence (revert to the pre-card text), drop just the callbacks clause
  (keeping the `router_settings` check), strip the identifiers from rule 2 and
  from the NOTE sentence, scatter the identifiers into a far paragraph that
  names neither the config nor the strategy (whole-file substring presence is
  satisfied; per-sentence scoping is what catches it), drop the config path from
  step 4, and five guard-side mutants — rename the handler, prose-ify the dotted
  identifiers (caught by the anti-vacuity floor), prose-ify every code token and
  split the obligation across two entries (both caught by the shape selector's
  exactly-one assert), and a second `.yaml`+`.py` entry making the selector
  ambiguous. The two GREEN controls are a benign rewording that keeps every
  identifier and extra operator prose appended to step 4, proving the leg does
  not forbid the runbook from saying MORE than the guard.
- **The API launchd unit had no `ThrottleInterval`, so a failing unit respawn-stormed
  the error log.** `api_launchd.build_api_plist()` set `RunAtLoad` + `KeepAlive` and
  nothing else, so launchd used its 10 s default throttle. Since t_37948685 added
  `--tailscale` passthrough this is no longer theoretical: a unit whose bind is the
  tailnet *legitimately* fails at boot whenever Tailscale is down
  (`api_server.resolve_bind` refuses to widen the bind — correct behaviour that must
  not be weakened), and launchd retried it six times a minute forever, each retry
  appending a refusal to `~/.hscc/logs/api.err.log`. The unit now sets
  `ThrottleInterval 30` and `ExitTimeOut 10`, matching the daemon's own unit in
  `hscc_daemon/install.py` (`PLIST_CONTENT`) — same Mac, same tuning — with a guard
  test that pins the two units' numbers to each other rather than to two literals.
  **This changes the no-flag unit's bytes**, so the two idempotence/byte-identity
  pins in `tests/test_api_launchd.py` are re-pinned deliberately in the same commit
  against the `0d95403c` baseline (key order, argv tail, log paths and
  `EnvironmentVariables` stay pinned byte for byte; only the two keys are added).
- **`hscc api status` said "not running" for an API that launchd had been serving
  since boot, and `hscc api stop` had nothing to stop.** The serve entrypoint writes
  no `api.pid` on purpose, so both verbs were PID-file-blind — the only thing the
  operator got was a note telling them to trust `launchctl` themselves. The design
  call the card asked for was **launchctl-aware verbs (as a pair)**, not
  pidfile-with-ownership-guard: a pid file would still leave `status` blind and still
  could not stop anything, only turning "silently un-stops" into "refuses and tells
  you the command". Now `status` reports the unit's real state (it asks
  `launchctl print gui/$UID/com.hscc.api`, the same probe
  `hscc-bootstrap/doctor_supervision.py` already trusts for the daemon, so doctor and
  the CLI cannot disagree about who owns the job) and `stop` runs `launchctl bootout`
  whenever the job is **loaded** — a SIGTERM would be undone by `KeepAlive` on the
  next throttle tick even when launchd has no pid right now. A plain
  `hscc api start` keeps the old SIGTERM/SIGKILL path. Honest scope, said on screen:
  a bootout is **session-scoped** — the unit file stays installed and `RunAtLoad`
  brings the API back at the next login; `uninstall-service` is what removes it for
  good. Probing is gated (`_launchd_matters`): no unit file and no pid file means no
  `launchctl` fork, and a suite that forgets the probe seam gets a visible refusal
  (`_refused_launchd_status`) instead of reaching into the operator's live gui domain.
  The stale "will look stopped under launchd" notes in `api_launchd.py`, `api_cli.py`
  and `hscc-api/README.md` are updated to say what the verbs now do.
  `api_launchd.py` stays subprocess-free — its `test_install_never_loads_the_unit`
  opt-in guarantee is untouched; the two new `launchctl` calls live in `api_cli.py`,
  which already performed the SIGTERM.
- **`orch-waker` retried a dead orchestrator pane every 30 s forever.** Board
  `pontaje` has a `pontaje-orch` profile directory but no tmux REPL pane, and
  `resolve_orch()` only checked the profile dir — so every tick attempted the
  delivery, every attempt failed with `no tmux pane running a Hermes REPL for
  profile 'pontaje-orch'`, `pending` never drained, and
  `~/.hscc/state/orch_waker.jsonl` grew one identical failure line per tick
  (125/125 identical since the daemon start). Two fixes:
  (1) the waker's config (`~/.hscc/orch_waker.json`, hot-reloaded every tick)
  gains `orch_map` — `{"<board>": "<profile>"}` — consulted before the
  `<board>-orch` convention, so a board whose orchestrator REPL runs under a
  differently-named profile is reachable; a map entry naming a profile that
  does not exist on disk falls back to the convention instead of going dark.
  (2) dead-pane backoff: after `fail_threshold` (default 3) *consecutive*
  failed attempts to one board, that board is skipped for `backoff_s`
  (default 900 s) — no inject attempt, no audit line (the audit is an evidence
  trail, not a 30 s spool), one `LOG` line on entering backoff, and pending
  keeps batching. A successful delivery, a changed `orch_map` or the expiry of
  the window resets/retires the counters.
- **An unknown fragment `kind:` is now a hard gate failure (exit 2), and
  `Docs` is the 8th legal kind.** `parse_fragment` accepted any kind:
  `kind_sort_key` parked unknown words in a catch-all bucket and
  `render`/`release` emitted a `### <kind>` heading per bucket, so an author's
  invented word became permanent CHANGELOG vocabulary — `[2.15.0]` shipped
  `### schema` (8 entries), `### Test` (1) and `### Docs` (6). The docs
  contradicted each other (a closed allowlist vs "unknown kinds alphabetically
  after that"), so nothing said no. Per the operator's decision on
  `t_f48f84c4`: a new `validate_kind()` runs in the parse pass next to
  `validate_entry_body` — reached through `load_entries`, so `check`, `sync`,
  `render`, `list` and `release` all refuse, and the release path that minted
  the headings is included — and `add_entry` validates `--kind` too, so
  `add --kind schema` fails where it is typed. Exit 2 ("malformed fragment")
  per the module's existing contract; the error names the file, the bad kind,
  and the legal names. `KIND_ORDER` is the closed vocabulary: the 7 canonical
  kinds plus `Docs` (last, after `Verified`) for doc-only changes — admitted
  deliberately because doc-only changes had no legal outlet and authors kept
  improvising (`t_9e45955c` wrote `kind: Docs` again after the audit).
  `schema`/`Test` stay illegal; a new kind now requires a deliberate
  `KIND_ORDER` edit. Blast radius zero: `load_entries` globs non-recursively
  and `release` archives consumed fragments, so no existing or historical
  fragment can fail the gate. `changelog.d/README.md` (both contradicting
  sites) and the kanban-worker skill now state the closed list and the
  hard-failure rule in one voice.

  Eight named tests pin the rule: fresh profile NOT written unless seeded;
  seeded missing profile IS created (`created` flips true once); `["*"]` =

- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_api_launchd.py`: 17 -> **30** cases (argv tail, byte-

- `hscc-api/tests/test_api_server_entrypoint.py`: **10** new cases — the only

- `hermes plugins doctor hscc-cluster` on the repo tree: **zero WARNs**

- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_plugin_manifest_drift.py`: 22 → **24** cases. The

- `bash scripts/run_tests.sh hscc-cluster` and the `hscc_daemon` leg green;

- `hscc-cluster/tests/test_discovery.py`: 26 -> **32** cases, green. The new
  `TestCachePreservesOperatorKeys` seeds `node_recovery` + a
  `target_profiles`-shaped key + a key discovery has never heard of, runs

  with the untouched `node_recovery.node_recovery_config()` reader (a

  Mutation-probed: reverting the carry-forward in a throwaway clone fails 3
  cases, and silencing the corrupt-file report fails 1; both reset green.
- `hscc_daemon/tests/test_orch_waker_dead_pane.py`: **18 new cases / 24
  parametrised runs** (map hit routes, map-to-missing-profile falls back to the
  convention, backoff arms at exactly N, zero attempts + zero audit lines inside

- `scripts/tests/test_changelog_fragments.py`: 32 → **49** cases. One fixture

### Docs
- `install_autoreboot` / `install_notifier_mask` / `install_gpu_clock_cap`
  module docs and the `node_recovery.NODE_RECOVERY_KEY` comment now state that

## [2.15.1] - 2026-11-02

### Added
- **The daemon now detects and heals HELD-STREAM PROXY STALLS (the
  2026-11-02 incident) on its own.** Two stalls (12:27, 12:45) left LiteLLM
  holding worker streams on :4000 while ALL four nodes sat idle answering
  direct requests in <0.5 s (faulthandler proof: the frozen worker blocked in
  openai `_streaming` `iter_bytes`); `check_proxy` could not see the shape —
  its probes only ask whether the proxy accepts NEW work, which a stalled
  proxy still does — and each recovery was a manual `proxy stop` → TERM/KILL
  the lingering litellm → `proxy start`. New stream `proxy_stall`
  (`daemon_ops.PERIODIC_INTERVALS["proxy_stall"] = 30` + a `CHECKS` row — the
  cadence SOT, never a private sleep loop): a stall is declared only when ALL
  THREE operator-specified conditions hold — (a) ≥1 ESTABLISHED socket on the
  proxy port (local `lsof`, allowed: the proxy is THIS host's service), (b)
  sum of vLLM `num_requests_running + num_requests_waiting` == 0 across every
  serving endpoint from serving.json (via the shared
  `throughput.fetch_node_metrics` — never ssh, never local `docker ps`)
  sustained ≥120 s (4 consecutive 30 s ticks; streak in monotonic time), and
  (c) a 5-token chat probe through :4000 still SUCCEEDS. Any UNKNOWN read
  (lsof failure, unreachable node /metrics, probe transport failure) fails
  OPEN with a named degradation and resets the streak; an intentional
  autodown (`autodown.classify == expected_down`, the shared table — no
  parallel rule) makes the tick inert. Remediation on a confirmed stall is
  the operator's recipe THROUGH the existing proxy-control path
  (`health._proxy_repair_orphan`: stop → cmdline-vetted TERM/KILL → plain
  start → port-owner verification, every leg a bounded subprocess) under the
  heal lease, then one re-probe; at most ONE restart per 10 min, cooldown
  persisted in `proxy_stall.json` (epoch stamps, survive a daemon restart,
  carried forward on every stamp so a healthy tick cannot wipe the window),
  and a suppressed remediation logs + raises a `proxy.stall.suppressed`
  event instead of restarting. `hscc verify` gains the stream for free via
  the cadence SOT (staleness floor `max(600, 2*30+90)`).

### Fixed
- **A profile regeneration can no longer delete the top-level `onboarding`
  block.** `hscc bootstrap --yes` at 12:24:45 regenerated every profile
  `config.yaml` through `hscc-roles/generator.py:generate_profile`, and the
  regeneration silently dropped `onboarding.seen.tool_progress_prompt` from 47
  profiles: every worker's first tool call re-fired the one-time progress
  prompt, hung at "preparing terminal", and dispatcher spawns stalled until the
  operator restored 47 configs by hand and restarted the gateway (fleet healthy
  12:41). Root cause: `_read_existing_config` read back ONLY `compression` and
  `auxiliary` from the on-disk file, and `generate_profile` builds the config
  dict from the role spec and writes it wholesale — so any top-level key the
  generator does not emit itself (onboarding, and anything else Hermes owns)
  could not survive a regeneration. Fix: `_read_existing_config` now returns
  `(compression, auxiliary, onboarding)` and the config write site merges the
  on-disk `onboarding` block through a new `_onboarding_block`, the same
  operator-choices-survive polarity as `_compression_block` / `_memory_block`
  — existing wins at EVERY depth, `_ONBOARDING_DEFAULTS` (empty today) fills
  only keys that are missing, nothing existing is ever deleted or overwritten,
  and the caller's dict is never mutated. A profile that has no onboarding
  block still gets none, so fresh-profile output is byte-identical to before
  (verified by the regen-is-idempotent tests). `compression` / `auxiliary`
  merge behaviour is untouched — `auxiliary.goal_judge` being ADDED is a
  separate, correct new-feature change. New in `hscc-roles/tests/
  test_generator.py`: the incident regression (seed
  `onboarding: {seen: {tool_progress_prompt: true}, extra_custom: 7}`,
  regenerate, both subkeys survive verbatim), an additive-only companion (the
  rest of the generated config is unchanged versus a profile with no
  onboarding block), the fresh-profile case, plus unit coverage for the deep
  merge, falsy-value handling (`False`/`0`/`None` are preserved, not treated
  as absent), non-mutation and the `None`-means-write-nothing contract.
  Mutation probes (backup + restore, tree verified unchanged after): M1 —
  reverting the call site to pre-fix behaviour (`onboarding = None`) fails
  ONLY `test_regen_preserves_onboarding_block` (1 failed, 60 passed); M2 —
  aliasing the merge instead of deep-copying fails ONLY the non-mutation
  unit. The suite is not merely counting tests.
- **`scripts` leg red on this host — "sibling python3.12 failed the (A)-only
  pass: E402" — was a mis-reported DEPENDENCY failure, and the cross-interpreter
  gate was non-hermetic.** No linter ever ran and nothing ever reported `E402`.
  The captured leg log (`run_tests_49013b1b.log`, `run_tests_t8438.log`) shows
  the sibling dying on `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'` /
  `'rich'`; the gate's `proc.stderr[-400:]` **character** cut landed inside the
  `# noqa: E402` comment on a source line Python echoes into a traceback, so
  the last 4 characters the assertion could show were `E402`. Three cards
  (t_49013b1b, t_84381a8b, t_9e45955c) each read that as a lint/order mystery
  and correctly failed to find one. Two real defects, both fixed:

  *Non-hermetic sibling selection.* The (A)-only pass imports
  `hscc_daemon.hscc` and `flightdeck.cli` at module level, which need `rich`,
  `yaml`, `pygments`, `markdown_it` from the **running** interpreter's own
  site-packages. `_sibling_interpreters()` checked only `os.path.exists`, so a
  bare interpreter became a "sibling" and then failed the leg — for reasons
  outside the checkout. Measured on this host: `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3.12`
  was a red leg until its site-packages gained `rich`/`pyyaml`, and green from
  that moment on with **zero** code change on our side. Selection now probes
  each candidate by loading the audit module itself (same file, same
  module-level imports; ~0.2 s per candidate measured) and drops a
  non-importable one with a recorded reason in `SIBLING_DROPPED`, surfaced in
  the skip message — so a host that has lost its siblings says so instead of
  failing a stranger's diff or silently looking green.

  *Truncation invented the error code.* Failure excerpts now come from
  `_root_cause()`, which reads whole lines and returns the exception line, so a
  `# noqa:` comment can never be blamed for a failure again.
- **`hscc stats`' per-profile tool view was silently dead: every
  `tool_events.jsonl` row said `"unknown"`.** `on_pre_tool_call` resolved the
  profile with `kwargs.get("profile_name", "unknown")`, but hermes'
  `pre_tool_call` fire site (`hermes_cli/plugins.py`,
  `_get_pre_tool_call_directive_details`) sends `tool_name`, `args`, `task_id`,
  `session_id`, `tool_call_id`, `turn_id`, `api_request_id`,
  `middleware_trace` — and never `profile_name`. The sentinel was therefore the
  ONLY value ever written by live traffic: 4291 of 5829 rows in
  `~/.hscc/tool_events.jsonl` when measured, collapsing
  `tool_calls_by_profile` into a single bucket. `on_pre_tool_call` now falls
  back to `hermes_cli.profiles.get_active_profile_name()` when the kwarg is
  absent, matching hermes' own `kanban_db._hook_profile_name()` contract:
  an explicit non-blank kwarg wins, else the active profile, else `"unknown"`
  only when hermes_cli is genuinely unresolvable. A blank/None kwarg counts as
  not sent. The lookup uses the repo's established Hermes-import fence
  (`profile_roster._hermes_gate` / `autodown`): import `hermes_cli`, on failure
  retry once with `HERMES_AGENT_PATH` on `sys.path`, and return `None` on ANY
  remaining failure — this runs on the hot path of every tool call in every
  profile, so it must never raise into the tool.
  Same file also stopped a second leak: `test_never_raises_on_io_error` patched
  no log path, so each `run_tests.sh` run appended a `profile_name="test"` row
  to the operator's live ledger (1538 such rows measured) — the same defect
  class t_1497a937 fixed for the completion/blocked ledgers.
- **check_dgx runs once per tick, not once per caller (proxy-stall c8-3).**

  `check_dgx` is the daemon's most expensive probe: two SSH round-trips plus two
  sparkrun status sweeps. During the 2026-10-31 proxy-stall episode it ran from
  several in-process callers at once — its own 60 s stream thread **and**
  `pipeline_watchdog` every 30 s (`dgx_ok = check_dgx_fn()`,
  `lifecycle.py:523`) — which is why a stream declared at 60 s was measured
  ticking at a ~24 s median, why the sweeps piled up on a box that was already
  struggling, and why the same `FLEET VISIBILITY LOST` WARN was re-printed by
  every caller (two WARNs 0.50 s apart: one tick cannot emit two).

  Now only the dedicated `dgx` stream thread runs the check. `check_dgx`
  publishes its verdict into a process-wide cache on every run, and the
  watchdog's default DGX signal is `health.dgx_verdict()` — a read of that
  published verdict, which performs no shell-out at all. The verdict the
  watchdog consumes is byte-identical to what `check_dgx` returned and what
  `~/.hscc/state/dgx.json` carries, so the restart/breaker semantics are
  unchanged; the 30 s caller simply stops re-running a 40-second shell-out to
  re-derive an answer it could read.

  Two honest deviations, both deliberate:

  - **UNKNOWN is kept a third state, not folded into a bool.** With the watchdog
    no longer running the check, a tick can find *no verdict at all* — the 30 s
    loop outruns the 60 s `dgx` thread's first run in the ~60 s after daemon
    start. Folding that into `False` would count a startup tick as a full
    pipeline failure (a vLLM stop/relaunch, and after three ticks — 90 s, before
    `dgx` has likely ever run — a pipeline block plus a critical notification);
    folding it into `True` would swallow a genuine gateway failure. So the signal
    returns `None` for unknown and the cycle forks: gateway healthy ⇒ an honest
    no-failure tick that stamps `dgx: None` rather than claiming a verdict it
    never had; gateway failed ⇒ still a failure, still stamped `ok: False`. A
    verdict older than `2 x cadence + 30 s` (derived from
    `PERIODIC_INTERVALS["dgx"]`, the same shape verify's staleness rule uses) is
    carried with a WARN naming the age rather than read as a failure — the audit
    measured a legitimate 157.85 s sweep, and stream liveness already has an
    owner that reports it instead of acting on it: verify's per-stream rule goes
    RED on a dark `dgx` stream.
  - **`trigger_engine` never ran the DGX check.** It accepted
    `check_dgx_fn`/`check_gateway_fn` and never invoked them (0 call sites in
    `trigger.py`), but `daemon_ops.py` wired `check_dgx` in, which is what led
    the audit to count a 15 s caller. The dead `check_dgx_fn` wiring is removed
    so no future reader — or caller — can multiply the sweep from that path.

  `hscc check watchdog` is unchanged for the operator: the CLI seeds the verdict
  by running the DGX check first (`cli._cli_watchdog_with_dgx`), because a CLI
  process has no `dgx` stream thread to publish one. `hscc check all` is
  strictly cheaper than before — the `dgx` and `watchdog` entries used to run two
  full sweeps back to back and now share one.
- **The pipeline breaker's alarm no longer claims a streak it never
  measured.** The reason string on the 3-failure block read
  `3 consecutive failures in 10min`, but the counter is a **time window**:
  `cleanup_old_failures()` prunes purely by timestamp and the success path
  resets `failed_count` without removing failure entries, so a healthy tick
  between two faults does not reset the breaker. Probed on main: DGX fail,
  fail, HEALTHY, fail -> blocked, and the critical desktop notification said
  "3 consecutive" about a history in which one of the four ticks was
  healthy. The card asked which of the two — behaviour or wording — is
  wrong, and the behaviour wins: the function's own docstring ("block on 3
  failures"), the 2.14.0 changelog ("the 3-failures-in-10min pipeline
  breaker") and the `len(recent) >= 3` gate all describe a window, the latch
  is a self-clearing backoff (so escalating a flapping-but-self-healed
  pipeline costs one notification + 10 quiet minutes), and a true streak
  would let a gateway that dies for 30 s every 40 s never escalate at all.
  The string now reads `<N> failures within 10min`, with `N` the actual
  in-window count instead of a hardcoded `3`, so the alarm text matches the
  measurement that fired it. Both legs share the one line that builds it —
  neither leg gained a reset rule.
- **The `doctor` budget-hook row now says WHY it is red: "this home never
  carried the payload" vs "the wiring was lost".** t_ba14f77f made a
  profile-scoped home answer only from its own `<profile>/plugins`, so a home
  whose tree has no `hscc-cluster` began reading red — the honest verdict
  (Hermes discovers user plugins at `get_hermes_home()/plugins` only,
  `hermes_cli/plugins_discovery.py:184`, so such a home loads no hscc plugin at
  all: neither the `[budget]` hook nor the hscc tools). But it read red in the
  same words as the failure the row exists to catch: when no candidate root
  carried an importable `budget_watch.py`, the row printed
  `budget_watch.py not importable … wiring cannot be verified` whether the
  payload had lost its wiring or had never been deployed. Measured before this
  change (real `doctor._budget_plugin_dirs` + `_load_budget_watch` +
  `budget_watch.doctor_check`, `HOME` untouched): `~/.hermes`,
  `profiles/backend-engineer` and `profiles/hscc-orch` green; every other
  profile home red — and the red set is NOT other projects' noise. Against
  `hermes kanban --board hscc assignees`, the red homes include ones the
  dispatcher has really run cards in (ios-engineer done=139, worker done=41,
  devops-engineer done=25, reviewer done=19, coder done=7):
  `install_payload._named_profile_plugins_dirs` only writes into a profile that
  ALREADY has a `plugins/` dir, so 47 of 49 profile dirs never received the
  payload. The card's (a)-or-(b) question resolves to (b): a real deploy gap.
  Decision: a never-deployed home stays RED — softening it to a warning or a
  skip would hide the gap — but it now prints
  `no hscc-cluster payload in this home: … never received the payload` with a
  fix that says to deploy the payload (or to accept it, if the home is
  deliberately not an HSCC one), while the lost-wiring class keeps its
  "not importable … cannot be verified" / "does not register the budget hooks"
  wording untouched. The card's two options collapse into one change: honest
  red everywhere, readable at a glance. Note the row-level verdict differs from
  the parent card's probe, which called `doctor_check` directly: through the
  row, `_load_budget_watch` short-circuits first, so an absent payload printed
  the *import* message, never doctor_check's "plugin dir not found under the
  checked plugin roots". The branch is in the row (`_home_has_hscc_cluster_payload`,
  a dir-exists test over the same resolved roots) because that is the only
  caller that knows which of the two reds it holds; the wiring verdict itself
  stays in `budget_watch.doctor_check` (verdict-with-feature, unchanged).
- **A slow node no longer reads as "the fleet is gone", and one outage no longer
  costs 35 alarms.** `FLEET VISIBILITY LOST` was asserted on the **first** failed
  sparkrun sweep and re-printed by **every caller** of it, so the 2026-10-30
  slow-node window logged 35 `LOST` lines across 35 minutes while `/health` stayed
  `3/3 online` and Workers stayed `3/3` (`docs/audits/2026-10-31-proxy-stalls.md`
  §7/§8 M2, proposal c8-2). Two flaws, one deliverable:
  **(a) the verdict had no memory.** A sweep that succeeded 5 s ago is information,
  and discarding it is what turned a blip into an alarm. Every **successful** sweep
  now writes `~/.hscc/fleet_last_seen.json` — `{as_of, epoch, hosts, workload_count,
  workloads}` — atomically (`os.replace` over a pid+thread-unique tmp, because
  `check_dgx` can be entered by several callers per tick and a fixed tmp name lets
  one writer's rename take another's tmp), and a **failed** sweep reads the age back
  off that file and publishes `fleet_visibility: "stale (last good 4 m 10 s ago)"`.
  The age comes from **disk, not an in-process clock**: that is what lets the verdict
  survive a daemon restart *mid-outage*, where a failure counter would reset to zero
  and a file already an hour old would look fresh (pinned by
  `test_aged_snapshot_from_a_previous_process_is_loss_on_tick_one`). sparkrun already
  leaves a running snapshot for the same reason (`orchestration/job_metadata.py:765-801`)
  and we deliberately do **not** read it: that file is sparkrun's per-job state, and
  inferring "no workloads" from a file we do not own is the fail-open this check
  exists to close. No sparkrun change needed.
  **(b) the alarm was per-call, not per-transition.** Loss is now a **threshold** —
  `FLEET_LOST_AFTER_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES` = 3 failed sweeps in a row (~3 min of the
  60 s `dgx` tick), **or** the snapshot aged past `FLEET_STALE_LOST_AFTER_S` = 300 s,
  **or** no snapshot has ever been written. The third case keeps the old fail-closed
  verdict verbatim, so a daemon that has never seen the fleet can never be made green
  by this change. The hard line prints **once per outage** (latched) and the next
  good sweep prints the matching `FLEET VISIBILITY RECOVERED` — an alarm that can
  fire but never clear is the same bug class as one that fires 35 times.
  Kept deliberately unchanged: the stream stays **RED** while degraded (an
  unverified workload list is not a healthy read, stale or not), so the trigger
  engine's `state.dgx.degraded` pseudo-event, `check_dgx`'s `serving_ok` vs
  `publish_ok` split, and the watchdog's auto-heal semantics are untouched. The two
  published `fleet_visibility` strings `"ok"` and `"degraded"` keep their exact
  values; staleness is one **additive** shape. Two kinds of "evidence" are rejected
  as evidence: the status script's `if not hosts` early exit (`{"host_list": []}` —
  stamping that fresh would let broken host resolution keep the fleet looking good
  **forever**), and a snapshot that is unparsable or stamped in the future beyond a
  60 s clock tolerance. Both fail closed. Env overrides
  `HSCC_FLEET_STALE_LOST_AFTER_S` / `HSCC_FLEET_LOST_AFTER_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES`.
  The log-completion line also stops over-claiming: it said
  `fleet visibility lost (sparkrun unreachable)` for *any* degraded tick, so the same
  over-claim survived one line past the alarm itself; it now echoes the actual verdict.
- **A gateway-only outage can now trip the pipeline breaker.** The watchdog
  recorded a failure entry and recomputed `failed_count` on *every* failure tick,
  and the gate that decides the block —
  `recent = [f for f in block["failures"] if not f.get("dgx", True) or not f.get("gateway", True)]`
  at `lifecycle.py:571` — counts the gateway leg explicitly. But the branch a
  gateway-only tick takes (`dgx_ok` fine, `gw_ok` False, the `else` of
  `if not dgx_ok and not intentional:`) was the only failure path that never
  called `save_watchdog_block()`. The appended entry lived only in the in-memory
  `block` and died with the tick, so every fresh tick reloaded an empty history
  from disk and `len(recent)` could never reach 3. A persistent gateway outage
  stamped `ok: False` every 30 s **forever** and could never latch
  `PIPELINE BLOCKED` nor send the critical desktop notification — the one signal
  an operator needs when the gateway stays down. The fix is the one missing call:
  persist the block on that branch. Intent was settled before changing anything
  (this card's DECIDE FIRST step) and the evidence says oversight, not policy —
  `changelog.d/archive/2.14.0/t_1c545ebb.md` describes "the 3-failures-in-10min
  pipeline breaker" that `check_gateway()` copies its verdict into, the `recent`
  filter already counts the gateway leg, and the block message reads
  `PIPELINE BLOCKED`, not `DGX BLOCKED`. Two properties are deliberately
  preserved: the vLLM restart gate stays behind `not dgx_ok`, so a gateway fault
  is fatal but never stops or relaunches the serving layer; and the
  intentional-autodown branch still does **not** persist, because
  `check_gateway()`'s `ok` is `job_ok and vllm_ok` and vLLM is stopped by design
  there — counting it would alarm during a deliberate power-save, the exact
  false-alarm class §5/C2 exists to kill. Probed to confirm the carve-out is
  real and not incidental: the `len(recent) >= 3` block sits *above* the
  intentional fork, and the three ticks stay at `gw_entries=0` /
  `critical_notifs=0` only because that path never writes.
- **`budget_watch`'s session leak-guard now evicts the least-recently-USED
  session, not the oldest-created one.** `_states` was a plain `dict`, and plain
  `dict` order is *insertion* order, so `pop(next(iter(_states)))` at
  `_MAX_SESSIONS` dropped whichever worker had **registered first** — an idle,
  stale session could be kept alive by a burst of freshly-created ones while a
  session that was still working was thrown away. The cost is not just memory:
  the evicted entry is rebuilt zeroed on its very next API call (`api_calls`
  back to 0, `armed` back to `False`, the commit baseline `base_ct` re-captured),
  so a long-running worker silently lost the `[budget]` note that is the whole
  point of the module — a worker deep in an over-budget turn, which is precisely
  the session that must not be forgotten. `_states` is now an `OrderedDict` and
  `_state_for` does a `move_to_end` on every touch, so the front entry is
  genuinely the LRU victim. The victim is still only a victim-selection rule for
  a leak-guard; nothing else in the module depends on the order.
- **The cold board scan is paid at most once per task, not once per eviction.**
  `_workspace_for_task` resolved inside `_state_for`, so the scan it triggers in
  a cold env (no `HERMES_KANBAN_WORKSPACE`, e.g. a session spawned before the
  dispatcher exports it) walked **every board dir under every board root** —
  and because the resolution lived in the *session state*, the leak-guard
  evicting that state re-triggered the whole scan on the next call. The
  resolution now lives in its own `OrderedDict` (`_workspace_cache`, same bound,
  same LRU rule): a task's workspace never moves, so an eviction can no longer
  re-pay it. A **miss** is retried after 60 s rather than cached forever, since
  a worker dir can legitimately appear just after the first API call. Two cheap
  exact-match lookups were added ahead of the scan (`HERMES_KANBAN_WORKSPACE`,
  then `HERMES_KANBAN_BOARD`'s own `workspaces/<task>`) and the scan itself is
  capped at `_MAX_BOARD_DIRS` (64) board dirs per root — now over **sorted**
  names, because `os.listdir` order is arbitrary and an unsorted bound would
  drop a resolvable task depending purely on how the directory happened to be
  laid out. Fail-open at both hook entry points is untouched.
- **A profile-scoped home no longer lets the ROOT plugin tree answer for it, so
  the `doctor` budget-hook row cannot read green over the hook the running worker
  actually lost.** `_budget_plugin_dirs()` contributed BOTH `<root>/profiles/<name>/plugins`
  AND `<root>/plugins` for a profile-scoped home, and
  `hscc-cluster/budget_watch.py::doctor_check` returns ok=True when ANY candidate
  dir is wired. Measured at the base commit: with the profile copy's `register()`
  stripped of the two budget hooks and the root copy intact, the row returned
  `ok=True` quoting `<root>/.hermes/plugins` — the deploy a profile worker never
  loads. Hermes' user-plugin scan is `get_hermes_home() / "plugins"`
  (`hermes_cli/plugins_discovery.py:184`) and under a profile-scoped `HERMES_HOME`
  that IS the profile dir, with **no fallback** to the root's; verified on this
  host against the real CLI (`HERMES_PLUGINS_DEBUG=1` parses exactly one
  `hscc-cluster` manifest, from the profile dir). The root copy
  `install_payload.install_payload_profiles` writes therefore cannot be
  authoritative for a profile, and letting it vote is what hid the dead hook —
  the same failure class the row exists to catch (a lost `[budget]` note nobody
  notices). Decision (strict, per the card): **the profile's own `plugins` dir is
  the ONLY authoritative tree for a profile-scoped home**; only a root-scoped home
  may be answered by `<root>/plugins`, which it still reaches via the ordinary
  `home/plugins` branch. The installer's write-both symmetry is untouched — only
  who may answer for a given home changed. The unwired verdict now also names the
  dirs it inspected (the green verdict already named its winner; a red row that
  names nothing cannot be acted on, and a profile-vs-root mixup is invisible
  otherwise).
- **`changelog_fragments.py check` can no longer pass a fragment that is
  missing its `---` entry separator.** Entries in one file are separated by a
  line containing exactly `---`; when an author omitted it, `parse_fragment`
  had no boundary to find, so the FOLLOWING entry's `kind:` / `task:` /
  `order:` headers were swallowed into the PREVIOUS entry's body. `check` never
  looked inside a body — it validates only the `[Unreleased]` *block* shape
  (pointer, or exactly what `sync` would write) — so it reported every fragment
  "consistent" while `release` materialised the bookkeeping lines as prose:
  18 leaked lines into `[2.15.0]` (5 files, repaired at `9ea52bc4` on PR #178).
  `parse_fragment` now calls a new `validate_entry_body()` on every entry,
  which refuses a body line that matches the tokens the parser itself consumes
  (`_HEADER_RE` + `_ALLOWED_HEADERS` at column 0) or a stray `---`, naming the
  file and quoting the README's vocabulary ("missing `---` separator between
  entries"). It lives in the parse pass, reached through `load_entries`, so
  `check`, `sync`, `render`, `list` and `release` all refuse the leak — the
  release path that turned it into CHANGELOG prose included. Exit code is 2
  ("malformed fragment") per the module's existing contract, not 1 (drift); the
  assembler and sync/release semantics are untouched — gate, not formatter.
  Prose that merely *mentions* the vocabulary stays legal (an indented
  ``kind:`` or an unknown word before a colon), and the pass already bites on
  the tree it landed on: `changelog.d/t_614f4cac.md` (from PR #180) had the same
  missing separator and is repaired here with a separator-only insertion.
- **The `doctor` budget-hook row checked the OPERATOR's plugin tree even when
  told which home to check — so a sandbox or `--home` bootstrap could read
  all-green over a broken deploy.** `_budget_plugin_dirs()` appended
  `~/.hermes/plugins` **unconditionally**, after the roots derived from the
  `hermes_home` it was handed, so the candidate list was always
  `[<named home>/plugins, ~/.hermes/plugins]`. Both downstream consumers then
  rescued the named tree with the host's: `_load_budget_watch` takes the first
  root whose `budget_watch.py` imports (a broken or missing module in the named
  tree fell through to the live one) and
  `hscc-cluster/budget_watch.py::doctor_check` calls ANY wired candidate green
  (an unwired named tree was rescued by a wired live one). The row answered
  `wired in ~/.hermes/plugins` about a tree nobody asked about — the same
  HERMES_HOME/plugin-dir resolution-leak class as the `importlib.reload()`
  HOOKS_DIR binding and t_444b1bb6's profile fallback, and the reason three
  `test_doctor_budget_hook` cases failed on any host whose own deploy is wired.
  The default root is now contributed **only when no home was named** (the human
  CLI path, which targets the operator's own deploy); a named home resolves to
  its own roots and nothing else. That tail was redundant in every legitimate
  case anyway — `home == ~/.hermes` dedupes onto it, and a profile-scoped home
  already contributes the root's dir through the `profiles` rule — so it bought
  nothing but the leak. Same fence as the waker / cron-watchers / supervision
  rows, and now honoured by the row that documented it.
- **`task_completions.jsonl` / `blocked_tasks.jsonl` stop recording
  unattributable rows, and the test suite stops writing to them.** 797 of 851
  completion rows (and 797 of 894 blocked rows) had `task_id: null`, so the
  fleet check could not join a single one back to a card. Root cause was not a
  hook payload drift — hermes' `kanban_task_completed` kwargs (`task_id`,
  `board`, `assignee`, `run_id`, `summary`, `telemetry_schema_version`) match
  the handler signature, and all 52 real rows in the ledger do carry a task id.
  Two `*_noop_without_context` tests in `hscc-cluster/tests/test_lifecycle_hooks.py`
  called the handlers with no args and no log-path patch, appending two
  all-null rows to the operator's live ledgers on every `scripts/run_tests.sh`
  run (73 rows on 2026-11-01 alone, against 1 real completion —
  `hscc_daemon/stats.py` counts any row with a parseable timestamp, inflating
  `completions.total` by 99% over 7 days). Fix: an autouse
  `_pin_lifecycle_logs_to_tmp` fixture in `hscc-cluster/tests/conftest.py` pins
  `_COMPLETION_LOG`, `_BLOCKED_LOG` and `_TOOL_EVENT_LOG` to `tmp_path` for
  every test in the suite (same doctrine as `_pin_serving_json_to_tmp`, so a
  test can no longer reach a live ledger by forgetting to patch); both handlers
  now normalise identity fields through `workflow._identity`, so a genuinely
  absent `task_id` is recorded as `"unknown"` and never a silent null; the
  auto-unblock scan skips `"unknown"` rows instead of chasing them as card ids.
  New payload-shape tests drive the handler through hermes' own
  `PluginDispatchMixin._invoke_hook_callback` binder, so an upstream kwarg drift
  fails in pytest instead of in the ledger. Verified hermetically: running the
  whole `hscc-cluster` suite against the fixed tree (1059 passed, 3 skipped)
  leaves `~/.hscc/task_completions.jsonl` at exactly the same row count — 857
  before, 857 after — so this suite no longer writes a single row to the
  operator's ledgers. Null rows did still appear during a later full
  `run_tests.sh`, from a SIBLING card's concurrent suite leg still running the
  unfixed code (the deployed `~/.hermes/plugins/hscc-cluster/workflow.py` also
  still assigns the raw `task_id`); that stops when this lands and the runtime
  copy is redeployed.

### Docs
- **Proxy-stall audit: corrected the `check_dgx` caller count**
  (`docs/audits/2026-10-31-proxy-stalls.md` c4/c6/c8-3, new c9). c6 claimed
  "`check_dgx` is invoked from **four** places" and c4 credited the ~24 s cadence
  to **three** callers; the real count at the measured base is **two** — the 60 s
  `dgx` stream thread and `pipeline_watchdog` at 30 s (one periodic caller on main
  since PR #182). `trigger_engine` was never one: it accepted
  `check_dgx_fn`/`check_gateway_fn` and invoked neither
  (`grep -c 'check_dgx_fn()' hscc_daemon/trigger.py` = 0, at the audit's own base
  `928e1aa3` as well as today), answering its DGX/gateway/NAS signals from the
  stream **state files** via `evaluate_trigger` (`trigger.py:129-146`). What made
  the misreading easy was wiring that looked like a call site —
  `check_dgx_fn=check_dgx` passed into the signature by `run_trigger_loop` — so c9
  records the lesson ("wiring is not a call site") alongside the correction. The
  audit's measured numbers are untouched and are not discredited by this: the
  ~24 s median and the two-WARNs-0.50 s-apart overlap come from tick timestamps and
  WARN counts, not from the caller count, and two callers explain them as well as
  four did. c9 also flags — without rewriting — that c6's "~112 extra
  checks/day" does not reproduce as a per-day figure (measured excess over one
  60 s stream is ~2,360/day, ~98-101/hour, so 112 reads as a per-hour magnitude
  with a per-day label); the pile-up it describes is real and larger than stated.
  c8-3's own proposal was also wrong in
  the same direction — it told the next reader to have `trigger_engine` read the
  state file, which is what it always did, and to have `pipeline_watchdog` read it
  too, which would have been a semantics change (`check_dgx` writes
  `ok = publish_ok` but *returns* `serving_ok`, `health.py:365-367` at the audit's
  base / `:512-514` today; the two diverge precisely during a FLEET VISIBILITY
  LOST episode). No code change.
## [2.15.0] - 2026-11-02

### Added
- **`hscc cards monitor [--live]` — watch every running card's worker at
  once.** One bordered panel per running kanban card follows that worker's
  transcript (the dispatcher's per-task log) in a single full-screen view; the
